name: The revival of Plato and genuine, first-hand classical scholarship
plain_explanation: The Renaissance's chief philosophical contribution was not new doctrine but the recovery of authentic, direct knowledge of Plato and Aristotle, free of the distorting glosses that Neoplatonist and Arabic commentators had layered onto medieval Aristotelianism -- and, crucially, the reintroduction of Plato as a rival to the scholastics' Aristotle.
precise_definition: Russell's assessment that the Renaissance 'broke down the rigid scholastic system,' 'revived the study of Plato,' and 'promoted a genuine and first-hand knowledge' of both Plato and Aristotle, hastened by contact with Byzantine scholarship, especially Gemistus Pletho and Bessarion, and institutionalized in the Medici-sponsored Florentine Academy.
why_it_mattered: This is, for Russell, the Renaissance's essential preliminary contribution to the philosophical greatness of the seventeenth century, even though the Renaissance itself produced no major original philosopher.
historical_origin: Hastened by the Council of Ferrara (1438) and the influx of Byzantine scholars.
examples: The Florentine Academy, founded by Cosimo and continued by Lorenzo dei Medici, devoted to studying Plato
Cosimo dei Medici reportedly dying while listening to a Platonic dialogue
competing_positions: The scholastic Aristotelian tradition it displaced
influence_on_later_thinkers: Set the stage for the intellectual ferment that seventeenth-century philosophy and science would draw upon.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Sponsored directly by political patrons (the Medici) and by humanist popes.
